chapter: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
title: Independence, Kansas: his father and the hoboes
summary: In Independence, Kansas, near the tracks, his father had hoboes chop railroad ties for wood in return for a meal; Chicago church is also mentioned.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Yes, this was the pattern of our lives right up until the time I left home, the fact of the matter is we lived in so many cities like I can recall it was a combination of various cities. Like we lived in Chicago at one time, which is a very large metropolis area, as you know, and my father had a very, very large church there that he was the pastor of. And I remember we would move to some small place like Independence, Kansas. You know.

You know. And I might inject a rather funny story about our stay in Independence, Kansas, and some of the things I remember in my life. My father had the reputation of being a kindly person, and they always -- there was always a lot of hoboes behind my back door, and knock on the door for something to eat or some sort of handout. My father would usually accommodate them by giving them something to eat. And this was common because we lived near the

railroad tracks, not too far from the railroad station, and you know there's an old saying that most of the black people in those days always lived near the tracks. You know, you could always find them by going near the railroad station, wherever the coal dust was (and) all those sort of things. Just below the tracks, you know, on the other side of the tracks.
But this was not really -- Said, I about
Yeah, you know, it isn't necessarily true.

And I didn't want to seem that involved in that subject. But the irony of it and the mirth of the story is that these hoboes found out about my father, that he was pastor of the church, and inbetween their stopovers there to get another freight train out of town, in and out of town, they would come by for something to eat. And my father found out that this was becoming habit, so the railroad company gave my father some ties, you know, to chop up for wood, which he would do himself most of the time because he was using our stove for heat and cooking chores.

And so then it got to the place where my father, as soon as these hoboes would come by for something, he'd say well listen, while my wife is fixing you something to eat would you mind chopping a few blocks. And in fact he even
taught me to do this, split these tiles with an axe.

Of course he would have them sawed, you know, the tiles, small blocks, and then it would be our job to split them. And I learned to do this when I was about 14 years old. You know, these are things he taught me to do. And I remember -- I never forgot this particular day, and in fact many times after this, you know, the guys would come by for something to eat, but while my mother was in the act of fixing the food, instead of them chopping the wood they would slip off and be on their way. In fact this sort of stopped most of them, they stopped coming by there.
That was quite a good idea.
Yes. It gives you an idea of my father's conception of how to have a little fun also.
